chunks: Ibn Mahboub, from Hisham ibn Salim, from Ziyad ibn Suqata, from Al-Hakam ibn Uteyba, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the fingers of the two hands and the toes of the two feet: 'Do you see that for what exceeds ten fingers or is deficient from ten in them, there is a wergild?' He said to me: 'O Hakam! The creation upon which the wergild is distributed is ten fingers in the two hands; so whatever is additional or deficient, there is no wergild for it. And ten toes in the two feet; so whatever is additional or deficient, there is no wergild for it. And for every finger from the fingers of the two hands is one thousand dirhams, and for every toe from the toes of the two feet is one thousand dirhams. And whatever is from paralysis, it is upon one-third of the wergild of the healthy.'

key_terms.أَصَابِعِ الرِّجْلَيْنِ: The toes of the two feet
key_terms.أَصَابِعِ الْيَدَيْنِ: The fingers of the two hands
key_terms.دِرْهَم: A silver coin used as a unit of currency in Islamic jurisprudence
key_terms.دِيَة: Wergild or blood money paid for bodily injury or death

ai.seo_question: What is the blood money value for each finger and toe according to Imam al-Baqir (AS)?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the Shia jurisprudence of *diyah* by establishing a fixed standard of ten fingers and ten toes, rejecting variable counts based on individual anatomy. It assigns a uniform value of one thousand dirhams per digit and introduces a specific rule for paralysis (*shallal*), granting one-third of the full value, which reflects the Imams' method of simplifying complex bodily injuries for legal consistency. This ruling underscores the principle that wergild is distributed upon the 'creation' (*al-khilqa*) as divinely ordained, rather than purely on functional utility.
